Gregarious

grih-GAIR-ee-us · adjective

Hear It

No recording available for this word.

What It Means

Gregarious is sociable; fond of the company of others.

The gregarious new student had already made ten friends by the end of her first lunch period.

Worked Example

Even on his day off, the gregarious shop owner spent the afternoon chatting with neighbors on his porch instead of staying inside alone.

Gregarious describes someone who genuinely enjoys and seeks out the company of others -- it's a personality trait, not just a temporary mood.

How Gregarious Sits Among Its Neighbors

Synonyms — open each to see how it differs

sociable

sociable: fond of company; friendly

Antonyms

reclusive

reclusive: avoiding the company of others

unsociable

unsociable: not enjoying the company of others

How Strong Is It? — friendly → gregarious → convivial

friendly vs. gregarious

friendly vs. gregarious: Friendly means warm toward others, without necessarily seeking out their company the way gregarious implies.

convivial vs. gregarious

convivial vs. gregarious: Convivial adds an extra note of festive cheer to gregarious's basic sociability, especially in group settings.

Build the Word

The pieces

root — grex, gregis

root — grex, gregis: flock, herd (Latin)

Put it together

Put it together: Gregarious comes from Latin grex/gregis, 'flock' or 'herd' -- describing someone who, like an animal in a herd, prefers to stay close to the group.

Use the root in a new word: congregate
